**Text:** 2 Chronicles 32:1-33 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 26:3; 2 Corinthians 12:9; Proverbs 16:18; James 4:6

Here is a man at his best. Hezekiah stands against the most feared army on earth, refuses to flinch, points his people to the living God, and watches the LORD win the battle without him drawing a sword. And then, after the deliverance, the same man stumbles over his own heart. The lesson is not that Hezekiah was weak. The lesson is that being rescued does not repair you.

**A king who fortified the city and fortified the people**
Sennacherib comes against Judah, and Hezekiah does the wise and faithful thing at once. He stops the springs outside the city so the Assyrian will find no water. He repairs the wall, raises the towers, builds another wall outside, and makes weapons in abundance. He prepares. Faith here is not passivity. He digs and builds and arms.

But the wall is not where he tells the people to put their trust. He gathers them and says, "Be strong and courageous, be not afraid nor dismayed for the king of Assyria... for there be more with us than with him: with him is an arm of flesh; but with us is the LORD our God to help us, and to fight our battles" (from 2 Chronicles 32:7-8). An arm of flesh against the LORD our God. He has built the wall and he tells them the wall is not the hope.

Then Sennacherib's mockery comes, and it is theological mockery — he stacks the God of Israel against the gods of every nation he has already crushed and says, where were their gods, what makes yours different. "And they spake against the God of Jerusalem, as against the gods of the people of the earth, which were the work of the hands of man" (2 Chronicles 32:19). And Hezekiah and Isaiah the prophet pray and cry to heaven. They do not answer the propaganda. They go over its head.

And the LORD answers. The angel of the LORD cuts off the mighty men in the camp of the king of Assyria, and Sennacherib returns with shame of face to his own land, and there his own sons strike him down in the house of his god. The wall he mocked could not save him from his own household. The God he mocked saved Jerusalem without one Judahite spear thrown.

**The sickness, the sign, and the swelling heart**
Then the chapter turns, and it turns inward. "In those days Hezekiah was sick to the point of death, and he prayed to the LORD, and he answered him and gave him a sign" (from 2 Chronicles 32:24). Fifteen years added to his life, the shadow turned back on the steps — pure mercy. And here is where the great man falls.

"But Hezekiah rendered not again according to the benefit done unto him; for his heart was lifted up" (2 Chronicles 32:25). The man who would not let his heart lift against an empire let it lift over a recovery. The same heart. The verse is exact about the mechanism. The deliverance did not cure the pride. It gave the pride something new to feed on.

The Chronicler tells us plainly what the moment of the Babylonian envoys really was. "God left him, to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart" (2 Chronicles 32:31). The trial does not put the pride in. It draws out what was already there, under the wall, under the prayers, under the great deliverance. There is no rescue so dramatic that it reaches the bottom of the human heart. Only one thing reaches that far, and it is not a sign on a staircase.

Mercifully, Hezekiah humbles himself, and the wrath is held back in his days. The pride was named and bent. But the chapter has done its work on us. It has shown that the strongest faith in the crisis can carry a pride that the crisis never touched.

**The deliverance that goes deeper than the wall**
I know this man too well, and so do you. It is easier to trust God when the Assyrian is at the gate than when the danger has passed and the wealth has come and the name is honored. In the emergency I have prayed with everything in me. In the season after the answered prayer I have quietly assumed the answer was about me. Pride does not feed on our defeats. It feeds on our deliverances. I have watched my own heart lift over the very mercies that should have laid it down.

"God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble" (James 4:6). "Pride goeth before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall" (Proverbs 16:18). The wall did not save Sennacherib and recovery did not save Hezekiah's heart, because the human heart needs a deliverance that goes deeper than the city gate.

That deliverance came in a King who was tried and never lifted His heart. Where Hezekiah, given fifteen years, swelled with pride, Christ, given all authority in heaven and earth, "made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant." The strength of God was made perfect not in a wall but in a cross, in weakness, in a Man who would not grasp. "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9).

The true Temple did not need fifteen added years; He laid down the years He had. And He keeps the heart that no recovery can keep. "Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee" (Isaiah 26:3) — stayed, not lifted. The cure for the swelling heart is a King who emptied His.

Deliverance does not cure pride.

## No One Is Past Return
*The worst king Judah ever knew became its loudest proof that grace runs further than ruin.*

**Text:** 2 Chronicles 33:1-25 · **Supporting:** Psalm 51:17; Luke 23:42-43; 1 Timothy 1:15; Isaiah 55:7

If you want to find the edge of God's mercy, you will not find it here. Manasseh is the case built to break the rule. The longest reign in Judah and the worst, a king who undid everything his father Hezekiah built and filled the city with blood. If grace reaches him, it reaches anyone. And it does.

**A reign of undoing**
The Chronicler does not soften it. Manasseh "did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, like unto the abominations of the heathen" (from 2 Chronicles 33:2). He rebuilt the high places his father had broken. He raised altars to Baal, made groves, worshipped the host of heaven, and built pagan altars in the house of the LORD — in the very house Hezekiah reopened. He passed his children through the fire in the valley of Hinnom. He used divination, dealt with mediums and wizards. He set a carved idol in the house of God.

Read that account and let the location land. The altars to false gods were built inside the temple. The house that had known joy not seen since Solomon now held a graven image. And outside its walls, Manasseh shed innocent blood very much, till he had filled Jerusalem from one end to another. One end to the other. This is not a king who drifted. This is a king who hunted the faith of his fathers to the ground.

And the LORD spoke to Manasseh and to his people, but they would not listen. The warning came and was refused. By every reckoning we use, this man is finished. He has had a godly father, a clear word, a full warning, and a long life to do nothing but evil. There is no account left in him.

We make these calculations all the time. We do them about other people and we do them about ourselves, and the Chronicler set Manasseh down in the record precisely to ruin the calculation. He is the worst case the book can hand us, and he is not put there as a warning only. He is put there as a door.

**The chains that brought him home**
"Wherefore the LORD brought upon them the captains of the host of the king of Assyria, which took Manasseh among the thorns, and bound him with fetters, and carried him to Babylon" (2 Chronicles 33:11). Among the thorns. Bound. Dragged in a foreign army's chains to Babylon. The strongest king Judah had seen is hauled off like a beast caught in a thicket.

And there, at the bottom, the thing no one expected. "And when he was in affliction, he besought the LORD his God, and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers" (2 Chronicles 33:12). Greatly. The same word weighed against the greatness of his sin. He filled Jerusalem from end to end with blood, and now he humbles himself greatly, and the affliction that drove Ahaz further out drives Manasseh home.

What happens next is the heart of the chapter. "And he prayed unto him: and he was intreated of him, and heard his supplication, and brought him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD he was God" (2 Chronicles 33:13). He was intreated of him. God let Himself be moved by the prayer of the worst man in the book. And brought him again. Back through the door. Back to the kingdom. The murderer of innocents, the defiler of the temple, restored — and the verse adds the thing all of it was for. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD he was God.

He came back and tore down the altars he had built, took away the idol from the house of the LORD, and commanded Judah to serve the God of Israel. The repentance was real because it reversed the hands that did the evil. He did not merely feel sorry. He carried his idols back out of the house.

**The reach of the mercy, measured by the worst man who tested it**
I have met people who believe their sin has finally put them past the door. They do not say it as despair. They say it as a settled fact — you do not understand what I have done. And I have felt the pull of it in my own heart, the quiet certainty that this particular failure is the one grace will not stretch to cover. The Chronicler put Manasseh in the record to break that certainty in us. "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise" (Psalm 51:17). Will not despise. Not the murderer's, not the idolater's, not yours.

"This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief" (1 Timothy 1:15). Paul called himself the chief; he had not heard Manasseh's case, or he might have given him the title. "Let the wicked forsake his way... and let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him; for he will abundantly pardon" (Isaiah 55:7). Abundantly. The pardon is sized to the sin and then larger.

And the door Manasseh came back through was opened by a King on a cross between two thieves, one of whom had nothing to offer but the bottom of his own ruin. "Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom." And the answer came without a delay, without a probation: "Today shalt thou be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:42-43). The true Temple was being torn down in that hour so that no defiled temple, no blood-filled life, no chained man among the thorns, would ever be past return. Manasseh was dragged to Babylon and humbled and brought home. We are dragged by nothing harsher than our own sin to the foot of a cross, and the King who hangs there brings us home.

No sinner is beyond return.

## The Word That Tore a King's Heart
*Reformation did not begin when the king got serious. It began when the book was found.*

**Text:** 2 Chronicles 34:1-35:27 · **Supporting:** 2 Kings 22:13; Isaiah 66:2; Hebrews 4:12; James 1:22

A boy becomes king. He seeks God before he is old enough to be told to. He purges the land. And then, in the middle of repairing the house, a workman finds a book that has been lost so long the king has never heard it read — and the reform that was already underway is split open by it. Josiah was reforming before the book was found. But it took the book to tear his heart.

**A boy who sought, and a king who purged**
"Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign... For in the eighth year of his reign, while he was yet young, he began to seek after the God of David his father" (from 2 Chronicles 34:1-3). Sixteen years old, and he begins to seek. By twenty he begins to purge — the high places, the groves, the carved images, the molten images, broken down and beaten to powder and strewn on the graves of those who sacrificed to them. He goes through Judah and into the ruins of the north doing it. The reform is genuine and it is thorough.

And it is incomplete, though Josiah does not yet know it. A man can clean the outside of the house with real zeal and not yet have heard the Word that judges the inside. Josiah is doing right. He is also doing it without the book. The high places come down by conviction; the heart has not yet been torn by the text.

Then, in the eighteenth year, while they are repairing the house of the LORD, Hilkiah the priest finds the book of the law of the LORD given by Moses. It is brought to the king. Shaphan reads it before him. And here is the moment the whole account hinges on.

**The tearing**
"And it came to pass, when the king had heard the words of the law, that he rent his clothes" (2 Chronicles 34:19). The reformer tears his own clothes. The man who had been breaking idols to powder hears the Word read aloud and the first thing that breaks is him. He does not file the book. He does not congratulate himself that his reforms were on the right track. He tears his clothes, because the Word read aloud showed him a wrath his zeal had not measured.

He sends to inquire of the LORD, and his words are a confession on behalf of generations. "Great is the wrath of the LORD that is poured out upon us, because our fathers have not kept the word of the LORD, to do after all that is written in this book" (2 Chronicles 34:21). The book is the standard he did not have. Now he has it, and it indicts not only the fathers but the silence the book was kept in.

The word comes back through Huldah the prophetess — judgment is coming on the place, but not in Josiah's day, "because thine heart was tender, and thou didst humble thyself before God" (2 Chronicles 34:27). Tender. That is what the Word does to a heart that does not resist it. "The word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword... and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart" (Hebrews 4:12). It found Josiah's heart and cut it tender.

Then he reads the book aloud to all the people, makes a covenant before the LORD to keep His words with all his heart, and keeps a Passover the likes of which had not been held since Samuel the prophet. The reform that began in zeal is now anchored in the recovered Word, and it goes deeper than anything Josiah did in the years before the book was found.

**Trembling at a Word we have not lost**
This searches those of us who handle Scripture for a living, and I do not exempt myself. I can teach the book without trembling at it. I can use it as a tool for other people's repentance and stand outside its edge myself. Josiah had an excuse — his book was lost. I have no such excuse, and on the days I read the Word without it tearing anything in me, the problem is not that the text has gone cold. The problem is that I have learned to read it with my clothes on. "To this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word" (Isaiah 66:2). Trembleth. That is the heart God looks toward, and it is the rarest posture among people who know their Bibles best.

A reformation that is only zeal will clean the high places and leave the heart untorn. A reformation born of the recovered Word goes all the way down, because the Word does what the king's hammer could not — it discerns the thoughts and intents. "Be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves" (James 1:22). The book read and not obeyed is the most dangerous possession a man can hold.

And the book Josiah found was always pointing past itself to a Word that became flesh. Josiah kept the greatest Passover since Samuel, and even that pointed forward — for the true Passover Lamb had not yet come, the faithful King who would not merely tremble at the Word but be the Word, who would not merely keep the covenant but seal it in His blood. Josiah cleaned a temple that would still fall; Christ is the temple that judgment fell on and could not keep down. The faithful Davidic King that Josiah, tender-hearted and young, only foreshadows came at last, read the law without flinching, fulfilled it, and bore its curse.

Tremble when the Word is found.

## The Fall and the Door Left Open
*The house burned. The book did not end in ashes.*

**Text:** 2 Chronicles 36:1-23 · **Supporting:** Leviticus 26:34-35; Lamentations 3:22; Jeremiah 29:10; Romans 11:29

This is the end the whole book was moving toward, and it is worse than you remember. The last kings come one after another, each evil, each shorter than the last, and the messengers of God keep coming, and the people keep mocking, until the Chronicler writes the most terrible four words in the history of Judah. Till there was no remedy. And then he does not stop there.

**Mocking the messengers till there was no remedy**
The final kings are a blur of failure — Jehoahaz carried off to Egypt, Jehoiakim bound to be carried to Babylon, Jehoiachin reigning three months, Zedekiah stiffening his neck and refusing to humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet speaking from the mouth of the LORD. The line of David is collapsing in fast motion, and underneath it the Chronicler names the real sickness.

"And the LORD God of their fathers sent to them by his messengers, rising up betimes, and sending; because he had compassion on his people, and on his dwelling place" (2 Chronicles 36:15). Rising up early. Sending again and again. Because He had compassion. The warnings were not the absence of mercy; the warnings were the mercy, sent early and often, refused early and often.

"But they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and misused his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD arose against his people, till there was no remedy" (2 Chronicles 36:16). Till there was no remedy. There is a place a people can mock past. There is an end to the early-rising patience of God, not because His compassion runs dry but because a heart can mock the cure until the cure will no longer be taken. The judgment did not come first. It came after the messengers, after the compassion, after the long refusal.

And so Babylon. The Chaldeans burn the house of God, break down the wall of Jerusalem, burn the palaces, destroy the vessels, and carry away to Babylon those who escaped the sword. The temple Solomon built, the house Hezekiah reopened, the house Josiah repaired — burned. This is the house going down. The whole book of the House has come to fire.

**The land that kept its sabbaths**
But even the judgment is not chaos. The Chronicler reads the seventy years through a lens that turns it from random catastrophe into ordered justice. The captivity lasted "to fulfil the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah, until the land had enjoyed her sabbaths: for as long as she lay desolate she kept sabbath, to fulfil threescore and ten years" (2 Chronicles 36:21).

The land kept its sabbaths. Centuries before, the law had warned that if the people would not let the land rest, the land would take its rest in their absence — "then shall the land enjoy her sabbaths, as long as it lieth desolate" (Leviticus 26:34). The exile is not God losing control of His people. It is the law doing exactly what it said it would do. Even in the fire there is an order, a faithfulness, a word being fulfilled to the year. The God who judges is not absent from His judgment. He is keeping count.

And a God who is keeping the count of sabbaths is a God who is keeping a calendar. Seventy years is not forever. A number with an end is a mercy hidden inside a sentence. "For thus saith the LORD, That after seventy years be accomplished at Babylon I will visit you, and perform my good word toward you" (Jeremiah 29:10). The exile had a back wall.

**The decree, and the King still to come**
The Chronicler had every reason to end in ashes. The house is burned, the people are gone, the line of David is in chains in a foreign land. By every law of how stories end in fire, this is the end. And he refuses it. He gives the last word to a Persian king's decree.

"The LORD God of heaven... hath charged me to build him an house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Who is there among you of all his people? The LORD his God be with him, and let him go up" (from 2 Chronicles 36:23). The book of the House does not close on a burned house. It closes on a command to build it again, and on an open invitation — who is there among you. Let him go up. The door that Ahaz shut and Hezekiah opened and Babylon burned is, in the last line, swung open again.

I have stood with people at the burned end of things — a marriage in ashes, a faith they thought they had mocked past remedy, a life that looks like a destroyed house. And I have felt it for myself, the conviction that this particular fire is the final word. The Chronicler will not let it be. He ends the saddest book in Israel's history with a man being told to go home and build. "It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not; they are new every morning" (Lamentations 3:22). Not consumed. The house burned and the people were not consumed.

Because the house was never finally a building. The decree to rebuild the temple was the first tremor of a promise that ran all the way to a manger and an empty tomb. "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" — He spoke of the temple of His body. The faithful King the whole book waited for, the true Son of David that Hezekiah and Josiah only sketched, came down into the ashes of His people, was Himself torn down, and was raised. The gifts and calling of God are without repentance. The exile had a back wall because God had a Son.

The Chronicler hands you a book that ends with an open door and a King still to come. The fire was real. The sabbaths were kept. And the last word was build.

He is not finished yet.
